result:
I would write about the moment before rain.

Not the first drop, not the darkening clouds, not the cold wind that slips through the cracks in the window. I would write about the stillness that comes just before all of that—the strange held breath in the air. It is a quiet so complete it feels like the world is listening to something it cannot name.

The leaves on the tree across the street do not rustle. They simply hang there, green and uncertain, as if waiting for permission to move. A dog lies beneath the porch, eyes half-open, and one side of its body rises and falls with each breath. Somewhere inside a house, a television murmurs low and blue. A kettle ticks. A child counts numbers under her breath. A book lies open on a chair, its pages soft from being read and unread again.

And above all of it, the sky begins to change in a way that is almost too gentle to see. The blue deepens by one invisible degree. The light turns silver at the edges. Shadows stretch, then lengthen, then seem to wait.

There is a moment when rain is possible but has not yet chosen to fall. In that moment, everything is suspended between dry and wet, silence and sound, now and after. You can stand on the street and feel it happening without actually being able to point to it. You only know because the air has become heavier, or because the birds have gone quiet, or because your own thoughts suddenly slow, as if your body knows something your mind hasn’t decided to follow.

If I could write freely, I would write about how that kind of stillness is one of the rarest things in the world. We are always moving through time, making things happen, filling every space with noise and purpose. But a moment like that asks you to stop. It does not demand anything. It does not ask for your name, your plans, your next message, your next step. It simply lets you exist for a few seconds without having to become something else.

Maybe that is why weather has always meant so much to people. It gives us language for inner states without forcing us to use it. We say, “I’m in a gray mood,” or “Something in the air is about to change.” We speak of storms breaking, of calm after chaos, of light returning. But perhaps the truth is simpler than we make it. We speak of weather because weather is honest. It does not perform. It does not hide. It arrives, lingers, and moves on.

So I would write about the moment before rain, and how it feels like the world reminding you that even the sky can wait.

And then, at last, the first drop.

One small, silver bead falling from the darkening edge of the clouds. It strikes the ground and makes a sound so faint it might be imagined. Another follows. Then another. The air shivers. The dog lifts its head. The leaves tremble, and suddenly they are moving all together, caught in a wind that has been there all along but was too quiet to notice.

The rain comes.

Not all at once. It comes like a memory returning in fragments: first the smell of wet stone, then the hush of falling water, then the city turning into mirrors. Windows sparkle. Puddles gather. The street below the porch darkens, and the world becomes soft-edged, alive, renewed.

And for a moment, the rain falls on the world as if it had always intended to.

As if it had been waiting all along.
